World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Live: Trump says Iran in 'state of collapse', US marines board cargo ship
World.content:
US President Donald Trump called out Chancellor of Germany Friedrich Merz and said "he doesn't know what he's talking about" when it comes to the conflict with Iran.

"Friedrich Merz thinks it's OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Trump posted on Truth Social. "If Iran had a nuclear weapon the whole world would be held hostage."

Merz previously said "an entire nation is being humiliated by the Iranian leadership" according to reports from Reuters, and that the Iranians were very skilled at negotiating.

German foreign minister Johann Wadephul posted on X, Iran must end its closure of the Strait of Hormuz and "must never acquire nuclear weapons".

World.title: Melbourne to Queensland exodus 'starting to see reversal' amid housing unaffordability
World.content:
With a full-time job as a civil engineer, Siddharth Nagar believed he was financially on track to becoming a home owner.

But six months on and dozens of auctions later, the 32-year-old Gold Coast man said it was an impossible prospect on a single salary.

"You either have to do two jobs or you need a partner with a really good income," he said.

A $1.5 million unit sale captures a growing house price problem A recent auction for a three-bedroom townhouse in Brisbane has captured just how much property prices have skyrocketed in recent years, highlighting the nation’s fast-growing housing affordability crisis.

Mr Nagar started house hunting in South-East Queensland (SEQ) last September when many units were within his budget of $750,000.

But he said within weeks those same online listings were taken down and re-advertised at significantly higher prices.

"In Logan [south of Brisbane], units were initially around $600k but then went up to $800k," Mr Nagar said.

"Here [on the Gold Coast] they were $750k, but started going for up to $950k."

He said the increase coincided with the October rollout of the 5% Deposit Scheme, which raised property price caps to improve accessibility for first-home buyers.

But in Mr Nagar's view, it incentivised sellers to match their asking price to the scheme's higher caps, which he said put homes further out of reach by increasing competition at the lower end of the market.

"As a first home buyer going into the market, there's always investors with an extra $50k in their hands … they're ready to overprice you any time," he said.

He said he had lost hope of buying a home on the Gold Coast.

"I think Melbourne is right now the only option for me [to buy a home] in Australia," he said.

SEQ under-represented in scheme approvals

Last year's expansion of the Home Guarantee Scheme — which allows for first-home purchases with just a 5 per cent deposit and avoiding lenders mortgage insurance, was billed as a measure to help Australians enter the market sooner.

Along with increasing property caps, it also removed limits on the number of people who could access the scheme and the income threshold for eligibility.

But in the rapidly growing market of South-East Queensland, those higher, albeit static, price caps have fallen behind — leaving buyers no better off.

Housing Australia data obtained by the ABC shows just 13 per cent of all properties purchased under the scheme in the five months from October were in SEQ, which takes in Brisbane, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast and Toowoomba.

Calculated per 100,000 people, SEQ's combined scheme approvals were about 90, compared with 132 in Melbourne, Sydney's 127 and Perth's 114.

Property analysts Cotality said with most SEQ property values exceeding the maximum cap of $1 million and shrinking supply, it was unsurprising the scheme had been rendered futile.

"When we look at the overall listing numbers … they've really been trending down quite rapidly over the last couple of years," head of research Gerard Burg said.

"So we've got a situation where there's a smaller pool of properties available for sale, [and] there's this increased demand that the scheme has allowed for, but there's just not enough opportunity there for a lot of first-home buyers to get into the market at the current environment."

Gerard Burg says South-East Queensland's housing market is not balanced with the scheme's price caps. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

As of March, none of SEQ's four cities had a median house value below its respective price cap.

And while units in some areas did, recent Cotality data showed prices of entry level properties grew much faster than those at the higher end since the expansion of the scheme.

In the six months from October, homes under the 5% Deposit Scheme's price caps rose at nearly double the rate of those above them, the data showed.

While that trend was also evident in Melbourne, Mr Burg said the city's relatively low median dwelling value of $830,000 gave it a "considerable affordability advantage" to SEQ, making it an increasingly appealing choice for first-home buyers.

More interstate buyers eye Melbourne

The Real Estate Institute of Victoria's Toby Balazs said a "disproportionately high" number of first-home buyer loans were issued in the state relative to its population size in the six months since the scheme's rollout.

Interstate buyers had mostly been driven to the capital, he said, with most targeting homes about $750,000.

Toby Balazs says a swell of first-home buyer and investor activity has come into Melbourne. (ABC News: Steve Martin)

"If you look at the median house prices say versus Brisbane, Melbourne is cheaper by approximately $60,000," Mr Balazs said.

"But really importantly from an apartment point of view, the Melbourne median is $170,000 lower than Brisbane."

While national property values have shot up faster-than-average since COVID, Melbourne's have been an outlier, seeing a growth of just 15.5 per cent in the five years to December 2025, compared to nearly 90 per cent in Brisbane.

Among the factors that contributed to the city's growth slowdown were its pandemic-era exodus of residents, the largest proportion of whom relocated to Queensland, exacerbating demand-supply imbalances through the Sunshine State.

Mr Burg said the migration pipeline appeared to be changing direction, though it might not be entirely in the context of housing.

"It looks like we are starting to see a reversal of that trend," he said.

"That relative affordability problem that both Brisbane and the Gold Coast have are seeing people drawn to markets like Melbourne."

Data shows entry-level homes have surged in price since the revamped 5% Deposit Scheme kicked in. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Migration gap narrows

ABS population data shows SEQ's net interstate migration has dropped by more than 40 per cent from 2021 to 2025.

And while more people continued to arrive in the region from the other states than leave it, it was far from the popular choice it was in 2021.

"That does suggest that fewer people are looking to Queensland as a destination and potentially more people are starting to leave," Mr Burg said.

Conversely, Greater Melbourne's net migration increased by 112 per cent in those four years.

Internal migration data has only been published up to mid-2025, meaning figures for after the 5% Deposit Scheme expansion are not available.

However, the ABC has seen dozens of anecdotal cases online of SEQ first-home seekers having relocated to Melbourne since late last year.

Queensland regional centres out of reach

While the scheme may have seen the most success in Melbourne, Mr Burg said more buyers were considering the regions over capitals than ever before for their first home.

But Queensland's major regional centres may be out of the picture for the moment.

The Gold Coast's property market is one of the most expensive in the country. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

"When I was in Brisbane, I thought moving to the suburbs or further away would make a difference, so I chose the Gold Coast, but the same thing's happened for the second time," Mr Nagar said.

" I don't know where else to go [but Melbourne]. "

A spokesman for Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said rapid growth in entry-level home prices compared with the rest of the market predated the expansion of the 5% Deposit Scheme.

"Without this scheme many first home buyers wouldn't be able to enter the market at all," they said.

World.title: Former ASIO chief raised questions about scrutiny of Bondi gunmen
World.content:
The former head of Australia's domestic intelligence agency questioned whether early assessments of Bondi Beach gunman Naveed Akram were sufficiently rigorous, while advising the royal commission examining the December terrorist attack.

The questions were raised by Dennis Richardson before his resignation from the commission as special adviser last month, according to a source with close knowledge of the inquiry.

The ABC understands Mr Richardson queried the thoroughness of ASIO's original 2019 assessment of Naveed Akram, and whether he and his father were reassessed in the years before going on to kill 15 people at a Hanukkah event in the name of the Islamic State (IS) terrorist group.

Mr Richardson also questioned whether agencies allocated sufficient resources to Islamist extremism after the national terrorism threat level was raised in 2024, and whether Australia's policy response kept pace with the threat.

Those issues are expected to be explored by the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, whose interim report is due to be tabled tomorrow, before public hearings begin next week.

The ABC understands the interim report identifies weaknesses in Australia's counterterrorism systems and responses to antisemitism, identifying further issues to be explored in hearings.

Sajid Akram and his son Naveed killed 15 people in their attack at Bondi Beach on December 14. (Supplied: Jessica Rozen)

Internal reviews by ASIO and the Australian Federal Police (AFP) have found there was no intelligence failure or negligence that could have prevented the Bondi attack.

Naveed Akram, 24, has been charged with terrorism and 15 counts of murder. Police shot his father, Sajid, dead during the attack.

Early assessment under scrutiny

Naveed Akram first came to authorities' attention in 2019, aged 17, while associating with several members of an IS cell who were later convicted of terrorism offences.

That year, ASIO received intelligence from a human source, codenamed Marcus, alleging both Naveed and his father had expressed support for IS, as revealed on the ABC's Four Corners program.

The former secret agent codenamed Marcus said he told ASIO the Akrams had expressed support for IS. (Four Corners: Sissy Reyes, file photo)

ASIO said it investigated the claims using its "most sensitive capabilities", but found them to be "unsubstantiated", concluding the Akrams did not support IS or present a terrorism threat at the time.

The ABC understands ASIO's internal review concluded the Akrams became radicalised after the outbreak of the Gaza war.

That followed earlier interactions with known extremists and travel to areas of concern.

ASIO director-general Mike Burgess told Senate estimates this year that the Akrams "went dark to stay off the radar", avoiding electronic communications and demonstrating a high level of security awareness.

He said a classified internal review, by an external counterterrorism expert, had supported its original assessment.

Naveed Akram preaching Islam in Sydney's west as a 17-year-old in 2019. (YouTube: Street Dawah Movement AUS)

"We stand by our 2019 assessment: the Akrams did not adhere to or intend to engage in violent extremism at that time," Mr Burgess said in February.

"In other words, many of the claims and criticisms being made about ASIO's handling of the case are baseless …

"The royal commissioner, of course, will reach her own conclusions."

ASIO has said it found claims by the human source Marcus had been "untrue" because he "misidentified Naveed Akram".

Marcus, whose relationship with the agency has become acrimonious, strongly denied misidentifying Akram, saying he met him regularly over many years.

Mr Richardson's intervention suggests doubts not only around the 2019 assessment process, but whether agencies revisited it, given the known risk that cleared suspects can later carry out attacks.

Travel, guns and monitoring gaps

The commission is also expected to examine whether the gunmen's international travel should have raised red flags.

In the years before the attack, the Akrams travelled to Central Asia, where the influential Islamic State Khorasan Province branch operates.

They also spent four weeks in the southern Philippines, a former IS hotspot, shortly before the Bondi attack.

Investigators suspect they attempted to make contact with extremists, but Philippine authorities have said they rarely left their hotel room and there is no evidence they received training or assistance with attack planning.

The hotel in Davao City in the province of Mindanao where the Akrams stayed during their trip to the Philippines in November last year. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Decisions by NSW Police are also under scrutiny, including why Naveed Akram was removed from a terrorism watchlist, why his father was granted a firearms licence, and whether security preparations for the Hanukkah event were adequate.

After ASIO's 2019 assessment, NSW Police interviewed Naveed and placed him on the Known Entity Management (KEM) system, which tracks people assessed as a potential terrorism risk.

But his listing was downgraded in the years before the Bondi attack, by which time he was no longer on the list.

Do you know more? Contact Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop on Signal: @seanrdunlop.01 and on Protonmail: seanrdunlop@protonmail.com

on Signal: and on Protonmail: Please use this form to get in contact with the ABC Investigations team, or if you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

The KEM framework is designed to identify signs of radicalisation or re-engagement by "known entities" who are no longer under active investigation, according to the National Counter-Terrorism Plan.

The plan explicitly warns that known entities can go on to plan or carry out attacks years after a "point-in-time assessment" finds they pose little or no threat.

Authorities can prevent people from travelling abroad as part of the KEM system.

The intersection between intelligence and policing decisions is likely to be a focus of the hearings, including how the Akrams were managed across agencies.

A 'highly paid researcher'

In 2024, Mr Burgess warned a terrorism attack was "probable" and was most likely to involve an individual or small group who rapidly radicalise and use "a rudimentary weapon such as … a gun".

Last year, he declared antisemitism ASIO's top priority "in terms of threat to life".

ASIO director-general Mike Burgess says the agency stands by its 2019 assessment of the Akrams. (AAP: Mick Tsikas, file photo)

Mr Richardson was initially appointed by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese after the Bondi attack to conduct a standalone review into intelligence and policing agencies, before that work was folded into the royal commission.

It is unclear whether his questions will be reflected in the interim report.

Investigating the return of the Islamic State terrorist group For the past two years, ABC Investigations has tracked the Islamic State terrorist group's revival in Australia, identifying key figures, mapping the network and raising questions about the response of police, intelligence agencies and governments.

After resigning as a special adviser in March, he said he had been treated as a "highly paid researcher" and feared he would have little influence over the commission's recommendations.

He also warned that Royal Commissioner Virginia Bell would take too long to deliver urgent recommendations about intelligence and policing agencies.

Ms Bell said in February that delays in obtaining material meant it was unlikely that the interim report would include final conclusions about the effectiveness of intelligence and policing agencies and the adequacy of security arrangements for the Hanukkah event.

Royal Commissioner Virginia Bell will deliver her final report by December 14. (Supplied: Murray Harris Photography)

The royal commission has a broad mandate spanning counterterrorism, antisemitism, social cohesion and the circumstances behind the attack.

It is examining the prevalence, impact and drivers of antisemitism, government and institutional responses, and gaps in laws and enforcement, alongside the actions of police and security agencies before and during the massacre.

The commission has received more than 3,500 submissions.

Public hearings begin next week, focusing on lived experiences of antisemitism, how it is defined, and how its prevalence is measured.

World.title: The link between viral hepatitis and one of Australia's deadliest cancers
World.content:
Dave Clune has no idea how he contracted viral hepatitis.

The only thing he's certain about is it happened sometime between wandering the streets of New Zealand when he was "six or seven" and meeting the love of his life as a "broken-up lad" of 16 at a nightclub.

It could have been sharing needles to use drugs or getting tattoos in his teenage years, living in and around Auckland.

Or perhaps, the childhood sexual abuse he endured back then.

The 67-year-old grandfather will never know.

Dave Clune at his home at Russell Island, in Moreton Bay, off south-east Queensland. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Half a century later, as he contemplates life listening to birdsong on the deck of his home at Russell Island, in Moreton Bay, off south-east Queensland, Dave shares his story to help others.

Chronic viral hepatitis has shadowed his life after a childhood surrounded by "a lot of domestic violence and alcohol abuse".

For information and support: Hepatitis Queensland information line: 1800 437 753

Cancer Council Queensland: 13 1120

Over decades, the virus scarred his liver, triggered liver cancer, and 17 years ago, he needed a liver and kidney transplant to save his life.

He's part of a campaign by Hepatitis Queensland to encourage people at risk of hepatitis B and C — both bloodborne diseases — to get tested and treatment.

Hepatitis Queensland also wants doctors to increase testing to pick up hepatitis B and C earlier in patients, prescribe treatment, and prevent liver cancer.

Dave Clune and Grace Trepels are about to celebrate their golden anniversary. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

By Dave's side is Grace Trepels, the woman he met all those years ago at Surfside nightclub, Milford, on New Zealand's North Island.

They are about to celebrate their golden anniversary, after racking up almost 50 years together.

Dave says his life changed "the minute I set eyes on her".

After years of living in and out of children's homes and youth detention centres, Grace brought stability.

Dave Clune and Grace Trepels met at a nightclub in Milford on New Zealand's North Island. (Supplied)

He quit drugs while still in his teens and started a family with Grace in New Zealand.

But it was too late to avoid viral hepatitis, which has stalked him since he was diagnosed in the 1980s while still living across the ditch.

Grace Trepels and Dave Clune. (Supplied)

Grace and Dave were both in their 30s when they brought their four children to Australia after facing discrimination in New Zealand because of Dave's hepatitis diagnosis.

"It was one particular event where children that were playing with my children were never allowed to play with them again because of stigma, and you can imagine the impact on those children," Dave recalls.

" Stigma's still around today, but not as bad as what it was. It was horrific. "

Severe illness from viral hepatitis has meant he's never been able to hold down a regular job.

Chronic viral hepatitis has shadowed Dave Clune's life. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

He and Grace have had to create their own employment opportunities mowing lawns, cleaning houses, and picking up scrap metal.

"People were always saying to Grace: What can't she do?'" Dave says.

"She was here fixing a chainsaw the other day. She could be taking the gearbox out of a car and then she'll be in baking cakes or making jams for charities."

A new liver and kidney

Dave Clune and Grace Trepels. (Supplied)

In 2009, after years of ill-health, Dave received a life-saving call — a donor liver had become available.

His immediate reaction was to throw up at the thought of another family losing a loved one.

During surgery at Brisbane's Princess Alexandra Hospital to transplant his donor liver, doctors realised one of his kidneys also needed to be replaced.

He woke up with a new liver and kidney — both from the same donor.

"After I had my transplant and got over the recovery part of it, and started walking around, it was like I was born again," Dave says.

"It's an amazing thing. It's changed my outlook on life.

"I realised how delicious life is. It was like I was in a new body. I'm not the same guy spiritually, I'm not the same guy physically."

Dave lost two brothers in their 40s to liver failure and he talks frankly about the toll decades of ill-health has had on his family.

'The relationship toll … I still don't understand why we're still here together," he says.

Grace Trepels and Dave Clune have been together for almost 50 years. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Despite effective anti-viral treatments, hepatitis B and C cause about half of all liver cancer cases across Queensland. Other risk factors include smoking, alcohol use, and being overweight or obese.

A fast-growing cause of mortality

An alarming new report, jointly written by Hepatitis Queensland and the Cancer Council Queensland, found Queenslanders are dying from liver cancer at more than triple the rate than in the 1980s.

It contains statistics showing Queensland liver cancer deaths have risen from 1.6 deaths per 100,000 population in the 1980s to 5.1 per 100,000 in 2018–2022, the latest data available.

"The steady increase in liver cancer incidence observed in Queensland mirrors trends seen nationally and internationally, where liver cancer has become one of the fastest-growing causes of cancer mortality," the report says.

Dave Clune was diagnosed with viral hepatitis in the 1980s. (ABC News)

It will be released publicly today and contains estimates that about 48,000 Queenslanders are living with chronic hepatitis B or C.

Modelling suggests 20–30 per cent of cases have not yet been diagnosed and "true prevalence may be underestimated", the report says.

Hepatitis Queensland CEO Anna Hawkes says Queenslanders most in need of care are often not receiving it.

"We have the tools to test, treat, and care for people with hepatitis B and C," she says.

"We're engaged, we're motivated to do the work. We just need to reach those that need the care. It's about equity and access.

"This report helps us to identify who is missing out and proposes solutions around what we can do about it."

Hepatitis Queensland CEO Dr Anna Hawkes. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

High-risk groups include those living in regional and remote areas, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, migrant families, people living in poverty, and prisoners.

The report says Indigenous Queenslanders experience 2.5 times the incidence of liver cancer and substantially poorer survival than the rest of the population.

"We can't reach elimination of hepatitis B and C, which we are committed to as a country, by 2030 unless we take everyone along with us," Dr Hawkes says.

Liver cancer survival among Queenslanders remains poor compared with most other cancers, although "five-year relative survival has improved from 8.6 per cent in the 1980s to 24.1 per cent in 2018–2022".

Dr Hawkes warns hepatitis C symptoms can be silent or flu-like, such as having fatigue and a fever.

"If you have had cosmetic surgery or dental work done overseas, a backyard tattoo or used drugs recreationally, even decades ago, don't ignore ongoing flu-like symptoms," she says.

"Ask your doctor to be tested for hepatitis."

Mena Waller is chief operating officer of Cancer Council of Queensland. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Cancer Council Queensland chief operating officer Mena Waller says Queensland has a clear opportunity to reduce preventable liver cancer and improve outcomes across the population, particularly among at-risk groups, such as First Nations people.

Between 2018–2022, more than 1,600 Queenslanders died of liver cancer.

Ms Waller, a Walman Yawuru woman originally from Broome in Western Australia, is calling for broader access to hepatitis screening, ongoing surveillance and treatment "no matter where people live and no matter who they are" to reduce their liver cancer risk.

"We want to see more community education," Ms Waller says. "We should be heavily investing in eradicating hepatitis and making sure that people are aware of the risks and the harms and understand what preventative activities that they can be doing.

"There's a simple test you can do to check for hepatitis and that can help prevent liver cancer into the future. It's a simple blood test."

Dave Clune does not know how he contracted viral hepatitis. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Key recommendations of the Viral Hepatitis and Liver Cancer Queensland Report include the development of culturally safe screening, surveillance and treatment pathways for indigenous communities; expansion of liver-related telemedicine services and outreach clinics across regional and remote areas; and more community-based hepatitis B and C testing in areas with high notification numbers and in high-prevalence settings, such as prisons and mental health services.

A Queensland Health spokesperson said the state's hepatitis B and C plans address the report's key recommendations.

"This includes boosting access to screening, early detection and treatment, and closing healthcare gaps in at-risk communities, including First Nations Queenslanders and people from culturally and linguistically diverse communities," the spokesperson said in a statement.

'The luckiest bloke in the world'

Dave and Grace moved to Russell Island about 14 years ago.

They bought a tin shed and built a house and garden around it.

Grace Trepels and Dave Clune in the kitchen of their home on Russell Island. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

It's become their sanctuary, put together with "lots of love and recycling".

"It's my therapy and it keeps me grounded. I'm very connected to this country that I'm honoured to live on," Dave says.

His health challenges continue. He has vision loss because of a genetic eye disorder.

"I live not day by day. I live foot by foot now," Dave says.

"If I have a fall, that will play massive consequences on me. But I still say I'm the luckiest bloke in the world."

World.title: Does the gas industry pay its fair share of tax?
World.content:
There is a question dominating Australians' social media feeds: Is the gas industry paying its fair share of tax?

Politicians, influencers and progressive think tanks are arguing over whether Australians are being ripped off by the current tax settings.

Industry representatives say they are being unfairly targeted, pointing to the $21.9 billion dollars in taxes and royalties paid last financial year.

But critics — including crossbench senators, energy analysts and economists — claim the system is not delivering value to Australian taxpayers.

Independent senator David Pocock has previously highlighted that the federal government raises more revenue from beer excise than the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT).

Advocates of a gas tax are proposing a flat 25 per cent tax on gas exports, or a super profits tax applied to windfall profits.

In response, the gas industry is mounting a multimillion-dollar advertising campaign to counterbalance what they view as misleading information.

So how does the tax system actually work?

How is Australian gas taxed?

Australia earns revenue from gas exports in three key ways:

The Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT)

Corporate tax

Royalties

Let's start with the PRRT.

Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT)

The PRRT is a profits-based tax imposed by the Commonwealth, which applies to offshore oil and gas projects at a rate of 40 per cent.

In reality, it has not been very effective at raising revenue, which is why Labor amended the tax in 2024.

The word profit is key here. Samantha Hepburn, a law professor specialising in energy governance at Deakin University, said gas companies do not pay PRRT until they have deducted their capital costs — a feature aimed at encouraging investment.

Chevron's Gorgon LNG project off the coast of WA, for example, cost around $70 billion to build and began production in 2016. The company made its first PRRT payment in 2025.

Chevron, which owns the Gorgon LNG project, made its first PRRT payment last year. (Supplied: Chevron)

"The uplift provisions have allowed significant capital and infrastructure deductions to be offset against profit," Ms Hepburn said.

"That means many offshore companies haven't paid much of that tax for quite a few years."

The PRRT raised about $1.3 billion in 2024-25, a year when LNG export revenues exceeded $65 billion.

The gas industry, however, argues the PRRT is only one part of its broader tax and economic contribution.

It also backs the idea of not having to pay PRRT until a project has recovered all of its costs, due to the high-risk and costly nature of developing gas fields.

This financial year, the PRRT is forecast to raise about $2 billion.

Corporate tax

Gas companies also pay corporate tax, just like every other corporation in Australia.

The peak body representing oil and gas companies, Australian Energy Producers (AEP), estimated the industry paid about $13.5 billion in corporate tax in 2024-25.

Woodside tells inquiry no projects 'would survive' with additional tax Oil and gas giant Woodside denies its business model is "weak" while arguing that paying a proposed flat tax on gas exports would kill the company's projects.

Sometimes, gas companies can avoid or reduce the amount of corporate tax they pay through various accounting strategies, such as carrying forward losses or claiming capital deductions.

Drilling for gas is a very expensive, high-risk investment, and sometimes a company's deductions are so large that they can cancel out profits for years.

For example, gas giant Santos and the Darwin-based Ichthys LNG project paid zero corporate tax in the 2023-24 financial year, according to data from the Australian Taxation Office.

Royalties

Another form of revenue comes via royalties imposed by state and territory governments on onshore gas projects.

Royalties are not a tax.

They are a sum paid to the government for the right to extract a public resource.

Typically, royalties are levied at a rate of about 5 to 10 per cent per well head value (the market value calculated at the point of production), but it varies across each jurisdiction.

In 2022-23, petroleum and gas royalties in Queensland and Western Australia alone were worth an estimated $3.7 billion.

That same year, producers made an estimated $36 billion exporting LNG from Queensland, and about $56 billion from WA, according to modelling from the Australia Institute think tank.

Like all other employers, gas companies must also pay payroll tax to state and territory governments.

Gas industry claims it pays enough tax

AEP has long argued the industry pays its fair share of tax, estimating the oil and gas industry contributed nearly $22 billion in taxes and royalties in 2024-25.

That includes $13.5 billion in corporate tax, $1.3 billion in PRRT, $6.6 billion in royalties and $492 million in other taxes.

Corporate tax is owed by every company in Australia and is not an extra levy imposed for extracting a public resource.

Samantha McCulloch says higher taxes on gas will make Australia "uninvestable". (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Gas tax advocates often compare Australia's export revenue to other major LNG exporters, such as Norway and Qatar, which rake in tens of billions of dollars every year.

But AEP argues that it is not a fair comparison, as Norway and Qatar have very different tax regimes and they both publicly own a large share of their gas resources, unlike Australia, which relies more heavily on private investment.

Chief executive Samantha McCulloch said assertions that Australia's gas industry was not paying its fair share were "demonstrably wrong".

"In contrast, higher taxes will make Australia uninvestable for new oil and gas projects, putting our future energy security at risk," she said in a statement.

The ABC revealed last week that, after much speculation, the prime minister had killed off moves to increase taxes on gas exporters in next month's budget, with timing among the key issues.

Will hiking taxes on gas exports deter foreign investment?

That all depends on how the tax is designed, according to experts.

The gas industry, federal government and the opposition have all raised concerns that increasing taxation — during a global energy crisis — could hurt Australia's reputation as a reliable trading partner.

They say a windfall profits tax would upset key customers, and investors, such as Japan, Malaysia and South Korea — the very countries now prioritising liquid fuel supplies to Australia.

Commodities boom left little to show, says Henry Former Treasury secretary Ken Henry says the under-taxed resources sector has hollowed out Australia's economy, and raising more revenue from the sale of LNG resources was in the national interest.

But Kristen Sobeck, economics lecturer at the University of Canberra, said a super profits tax targeting "excessive profits" should have little impact on investment.

"We can't really argue that would spook investors, because it's only applied to situations where no one can really foresee the huge profits that are being made," Ms Sobeck said.

Australia's LNG exporters recorded massive windfall profits in 2022 by taking advantage of global energy price spikes caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Ms Hepburn said long-term contracts with buyers such as Japan were already locked in and would therefore remain largely unaffected.

Last week, a parliamentary inquiry heard the United Kingdom had experienced a decline in investment after introducing a windfall tax on oil and gas producers in 2022.

But Australian Industry Group's director of climate change and energy, Tennant Reid, said that wasn't the full picture.

He said most of the gas in the UK's share of the North Sea had already been extracted, making it "hard to pick out the specific impact of that tax change".

Mr Reid also said Australian gas would be in high demand for years to come, especially given Iran's attacks on Qatar's LNG export facilities and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.

"Australia looks like an island of stability amidst all of that," he said.

World.title: Speculation builds on how upcoming budget will address fuel supply
World.content:
The global oil crisis sparked by war in the Middle East has dramatically exposed Australia's fuel vulnerabilities, sharpening calls from industry analysts for the federal government to secure future energy supplies.

Having secured shipments through to mid-May, attention is turning to how Labor will use next month's federal budget to shore up Australia's liquid fuel supply long term and reduce its dependence on volatile international markets.

The government has signalled energy security will be a key pillar of the budget, with members of the energy sector expecting fuel storage and refining capacity to be a focus for funding.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen has been careful not to close the door on these options, but two months into the fuel crisis, he has also refused to foreshadow any specific new measures ahead of the budget.

"It's no secret we're in ongoing conversations about fuel security and what sensible things can be considered," he said.

"There's a budget coming up. If there are sensible measures, the government will consider them."

Extra domestic storage capacity

A pathway to bolstering Australia's domestic fuel stockpile is widely anticipated to be a feature of the budget amid widespread concern the current minimum stockholding obligation of 30 days' supply of diesel, petrol and jet fuel is not sufficient.

The Strait of Hormuz blockade has revealed domestic supplies and stockpiles as a key vulnerability for the country.

Mr Bowen said on Sunday Australia had 44 days' worth of petrol, 33 days of diesel, and 30 days of jet fuel in reserve, just above the Minimum Stockholding Obligation.

Taylor makes pitch to double minimum fuel reserves Australia would have 60 days' worth of fuel supplies in reserve under an $800 million Coalition proposal that would cost drivers one cent per litre.

The Coalition has vowed to increase minimum stockholding obligations for fuel importers from 30 days to 60 days if elected.

That policy would come at a cost of $6 billion, with a 1 cent per litre increase on fuel prices passed on to drivers to cover the bill.

Australian Institute of Petroleum chief executive Malcolm Roberts said most moves to increase Australia's fuel stockpile would cause a fuel price increase.

"Any additional storage will take time to build and will create costs that will have to be passed on to fuel users," he said.

"So, there's a tricky balancing act here."

Reaching the 90-day commitment Australia has agreed to as a member of the International Energy Agency would, Resources Minister Madeleine King has previously said, "be an enormously expensive undertaking" and a massive proposition.

"It is estimated to cost about $20 billion if you were to store the suggested amount of fuel for that amount of time," she said in March.

Will refineries be funded?

A fire at Geelong's Viva refinery highlighted the vulnerability of Australia's onshore refining abilities.

While the government has talked down the prospect of helping to fund a new refinery, sector insiders suggest upgrades to an existing refinery could be on the table.

Earlier this month, the federal government announced it would open loans through the National Reconstruction Fund for sectors impacted by the supply chain shocks.

Chris Bowen has revealed little about what energy security measures will be funded. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

It led to some speculation the door was being left ajar for an announcement of government backing for a new oil refinery.

But the prime minister has said supply, rather than refining, was where his government's attention would be focused.

"We're looking, of course, across the board. Anything that we can do, any constructive proposals, we're open for dialogue," Anthony Albanese said last week.

"What we are concentrating on at the moment isn't something that is time-lengthy for obvious reasons," he said of the refinery question.

"What we are doing is concentrating on supply."

Australia's two existing refineries have been "working full pelt to ensure that supply is kept up", Mr Bowen has said.

In Brisbane, the Ampol refinery has been given $25 million by the Queensland government to produce renewable diesel to boost domestic fuel production and ease reliance on imported crude oil.

"You can drop in 100 per cent renewable diesel into an existing engine and use it, so it's not an additive that gets blended in, it's a genuine replacement fuel," Mr Roberts said.

While not an immediate fix to the fuel crisis, supporters of the project suggest Australia's other petrol refinery, Viva Energy in Geelong, could be a candidate for similar federal support.

The Queensland project is expected to produce 20 million litres of diesel every year at the Lytton oil refinery by 2028, and 750 million litres per year by the early 2030s under stage two of the development.

Institute for Integrated Economic Research Australia (IIERA) board member John Blackburn said biofuels were a "good pathway", "but it's going to take a fair bit of time".

A $1 billion pathway

Mr Blackburn said reducing demand would ultimately be the best approach to improving energy security, but conceded that it was a long-term project.

The energy minister said there would be some new money for renewable energy, but "no big new funding".

But Mr Blackburn said he would not be surprised by funding announcements around electrification.

Ampol's Lytton refinery has been given $25 million to produce renewable diesel. (AAP: Darren England)

"What you have to do is look at the whole thing as a system and, so, the very first thing you start to look at is how do we reduce demand," he said.

"The major way of doing that is electrification."

But he said that process would take decades.

Mr Blackburn, a former Royal Australian Air Force deputy chief, suggested a quicker process could be upgrading local refineries so they could process Australian oil and condensate.

An IIERA report indicated that work could be done for between $500 million and $1 billion per refinery and operational as soon as next year. But it would involve shutdowns.

"We export a lot of condensate, which is processed overseas in a jet fuel and diesel," he said.

"So there's stuff we could do there."

World.title: 'Huge amount' of antibiotics at salmon farm concerning, say Greens, expert
World.content:
More than 2.7 tonnes of antibiotics were used at a Tasmanian salmon farm lease in just two months, but the total amount that entered public waterways over summer remains under wraps.

The Tasmanian Environment Protection Authority (EPA) has released its report on the use of florfenicol in the Zuidpool lease in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel.

But the lease is just one of nine salmon leases spread throughout south-east Tasmania that used florfenicol over the summer.

Between January and March last year, more than 13,500 tonnes of fish died due to the bacterial disease piscirickettsia salmonis. (Supplied: Tassal)

Months after permissions to use the antibiotic were revoked, following detections in wild shellfish more than 10 kilometres away, state authorities still don't know the total amount of florfenicol used.

"It's a shockingly large figure and it's just one site," Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff said.

"Where else and why don't we know what's happening elsewhere?

" It's never been tested, the impacts on the marine life, and for that quantity to be going into waterways is an astoundingly high amount. "

The salmon industry has lost large amounts of stock because of the bacterial outbreak. (Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation)

Antibiotic resistance expert at the University of Queensland, Mark Blaskovich, said it was "alarming" to hear that 2.7 tonnes had been used at one site.

"That's a huge amount of antibiotics that are ending up in the environment," he said.

"The concern is that florfenicol is an agricultural antibiotic, but it's very closely related to a human [antibiotic] called chloramphenicol, and if bacteria become resistant to one, they become resistant to the other one as well.

"So, by pumping these large amounts of florfenicol into the environment, it potentially means that bacteria in the environment can become resistant and that resistance mechanism can end up being transferred to bacteria that might end up infecting humans.

" In Australia, resistant infections actually lead to more deaths per year than car crashes. "

A permit for the use by salmon producers to deploy AbbeyFlor florfenicol premix was issued, but later revoked. (Abbey Laboratories)

The salmon companies sought to use florfenicol to try and prevent another mass mortality event like last summer, where fat globules and bits of dead fish washed up on beaches.

Between January and March last year, more than 13,500 tonnes of fish died due to a bacterial disease known as Piscirickettsia salmonis.

Despite the use of the antibiotic this summer, 9,000 tonnes of fish still died in the same period.

That's roughly 2 million fish.

At a press conference last week, Salmon Tasmania chief executive John Whittington said the industry was still learning how to deal with the disease.

"This year we were successful compared to the first year it was here and we will continue to strive to improve," he told reporters.

Information not provided

The industry's permit to use the antibiotic was revoked on March 4, after traces of florfenicol were found in wild shellfish more than 10 kilometres away.

The Greens and the media have since tried to find out how much florfenicol was released into southern Tasmanian waters while the permit was active.

But questions to state authorities and the salmon industry provided no clarity.

John Whittington has defended the use of the antibiotics to combat the bacterial infection. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

Salmon farming licence to use antibiotic revoked The use of florfenicol in Tasmania's salmon industry has been banned as the country's veterinary medicine regulator suspends an emergency licence for the antibiotic.

In February, the ABC sought information from the EPA under right-to-information (RTI) laws about the total amount of florfenicol used in salmon pens, as well as a breakdown for each site and details of salmon mortalities at treated sites.

In response, the EPA said it "did not locate any information relevant to (the) request".

The Greens were also unable to obtain any information through RTIs.

After Dr Woodruff asked Premier Jeremy Rockliff for the information in parliament, he said he would seek the information and come back, but he was unable to provide the answer.

That's because none of Tasmania's state authorities, including the EPA, which is responsible for monitoring the industry, and the environment department, know how much florfenicol was released.

Rosalie Woodruff says the fact that the information hasn't been made public shows "an outrageous lack of respect". (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The salmon industry does have the information, but Salmon Tasmania's John Whittington recently declined to provide it, telling the media the EPA would be releasing it through a series of reports.

However, the salmon companies were required to provide the information to the Australian Pesticides Veterinary Medicine Association (APVMA) at the end of the permit.

The APVMA has confirmed to the ABC that it does have the information, but has yet to provide it.

Dr Woodruff said the fact that the information hasn't been made public shows "an outrageous lack of respect".

"It is so rude to treat people like fools because what it's doing, the drip feeding of information, is preventing people from understanding in one go exactly what's happened," she said.

"When we know that the information exists, when we know that the industry has it, the EPA could require, right now, the industry to give them that information and they could immediately make it public.

" The fact that they're not doing that is deeply concerning. "

Antibiotic used 21 times across nine sites

After traces of florfenicol were found in non-target species, the permit to use it was discontinued. (Supplied: Tassal)

Salmon antibiotic leads to partial rock lobster fishery closure The Tasmanian government closed two zones within the state's rock lobster fishery just hours after the commercial season opened. The closure is in response to concerns about an antibiotic being used by salmon companies and the rock lobster industry's reputation in overseas markets.

Professor Blaskovich said the information should be made public.

"Given that we don't know, we're sort of relying on the assurances that it wasn't going to be an issue and it wouldn't be impacting the environment outside the salmon farms, that's obviously not the case," he said.

"The more information we have, the better we can help to understand what the potential impact is."

While the total quantity of florfenicol used remains unknown to Tasmanians, EPA data shows it was used 21 times across nine sites.

It was used nine times at the Zuidpool lease — between November 11 and December 9. Each time treatment was done over the course of nine days.

Another report reveals that 553 kilograms of florfenicol were used at Tassal's Meads Creek and Stringers Cover leases.

Seafood industry 'breathed a sigh of relief' when permit revoked

The Environment Department has also confirmed that it has extended the closure of areas of the abalone fishery in south-eastern waters, which had been due to reopen on April 1.

The closure has been extended indefinitely.

How many salmon farms are there in Tasmania — and who owns them? Those black, circular things floating in the water off the Tasmanian coastline? They are salmon farms. Here is how many there are — and who owns them.

The fisheries were closed as a precautionary measure due to concerns that trace amounts of florfenicol could affect international trade markets.

"All closures are precautionary and provide assurance that Tasmanian seafood meets all relevant market standards," the spokesperson said.

"We continue to consult closely with industry stakeholders. The monitoring program will support fisheries managers to reopen fisheries when appropriate while also assuring markets that their requirements are met."

The head of Salmon Tasmania says the industry was still learning how to deal with the disease and would "continue to strive to improve". (Tassal)

Parts of the seafood industry are concerned that the salmon industry will "seek to use florfenicol in the future under a separate permitting process".

In Seafood Industry Tasmania's April/May edition, the Tasmanian Rock Lobster Council's Jane McGann wrote that the "entire wild-catch sector breathed a sigh of relief" when the permit was suspended.

Tasmanian Abalone Council's Dr Julian Amos, a former salmon industry spokesperson, also wrote that the use of florfenicol "has caused increasing concern".

He added that "the salmon industry is still keen to continue to use florfenicol and will be seeking a permit going forward".

World.title: The 'double-headed monster' set to push up prices at the check-out
World.content:
Plastic could become the next inflationary pressure on Australian hip pockets, as companies that make everything from milk bottles to cosmetics tubes battle supply shocks during the war in the Middle East.

The price of resin that goes into making plastic containers has risen as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, with refineries that process a by-product of crude oil into this material even declaring force majeure.

"We've got a double-headed monster," packaging company boss Raphael Geminder told ABC News.

"One is a lack of supply, and as a result of a lack of supply, price has gone crazy, because everyone's chasing a very small amount of raw material."

Mr Geminder's Pact Group makes hundreds of thousands of plastic milk bottles daily, for product lines sold in supermarkets nationally.

Raphael Geminder says his packaging firm has been 'scrambling like crazy'. (ABC News: Matthew Holmes)

It already informed its customers last month that it is "immediately" passing on its higher "costs of securing supply, including resin, freight and other raw material costs".

Packaging typically only forms a small part of a grocery product’s overall production cost — but the inflationary toll for manufacturers will quickly add up on low price, fast moving consumer goods.

Data provided to ABC News by Pact indicates the cost food-grade resin out of Singapore has shot up 110 per cent to $US1,920 ($2,675) since the war began. The same resin out of the US has risen by almost as much.

"We've been scrambling like crazy," Mr Geminder said.

White resin beads are used by firms like Pact to create plastic packaging. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Coles, Woolworths face packaging pressure, hike milk prices

Coles and Woolworths have already increased the price of their home-brand milk lines, with both supermarkets acknowledging packaging as part of the current pressure on the dairy supply chain.

Milk production declines as costs soar Farmers warn of slowing production.

"In response to the requests of milk processors for support to cover the cost of rising fuel, fertiliser and packaging, we have increased our retail prices for Woolworths own brand milk," Australia's biggest supermarket said.

Meanwhile, the farmers' cooperative Norco has informed its buyers that a bottle of milk is going up by 10 to 20 cents.

Norco's milk is sold in major supermarkets and is used by the hospitality industry to make things like coffees in cafes.

"We estimate the costs of hyperinflation just on diesel and plastics in our business to be about $1.6 million per month," Norco's chief executive Michael Hampson says.

Norco has informed buyers of price increases as fuel and plastic costs rise. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

From cows to cosmetics

The plastics price pain extends far beyond milk bottles.

Impact International, which makes squeeze tubes for the cosmetics industry, has also informed the major brands that it works with that it's increasing costs.

The cosmetics industry is facing increased packaging costs due to the Middle East war. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Impact's boss Aleks Lajovic said the current supply shock reminds him of those during the pandemic.

"The issue that we have now with this COVID 2.0 environment is that every single aspect of the supply chain is affected," he said.

"It's placing a tremendous pressure on our suppliers. It's placing a tremendous pressure on ourselves.

" That pressure will eventually flow through to the consumer in terms of availability and price. "

Aleks Lajovic, managing director of Sydney-based tube manufacturer Impact International. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Second round inflation impact still to come

Inflation data that covers the start of the war in the Middle East and its subsequent shock to oil prices will be released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics mid-morning on Wednesday.

However, that is only expected to show initial price impacts, such as the rising costs at petrol bowsers in the last few weeks of March.

Secondary impacts including plastic inflation might take a while to show up in official figures.

"I think most customers are passing on inflation in some form," Pact's Mr Geminder said.

"Whether it's in pure price, whether it's in some operating efficiency, whether it's in looking at how they promote.

"I think everyone is intimately aware that ultimately, you can only pass on price to a certain point."

Major food manufacturers are affected, with Nestle forecasting 'tighter supply conditions from as early as next month'. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Another major user of plastic, Nestle, has confirmed it has also been battling to contain the supply chain shock.

Loading...

"The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is creating disruption across global supply chains, including the production of some resins used to manufacture soft plastics such as food wrappers," Nestle's local manager of confectionary and snacks, Andrew Lawrey, said in a statement.

"While there is no immediate shortage of soft plastic packaging, we anticipate tighter supply conditions from as early as next month as suppliers face operational disruptions beyond their control.

"Like many food manufacturers, we're seeing cost increases across fuel, packaging and ingredients.

"We know many households are also doing it tough with cost-of-living pressures, and we don't take any changes that may affect shoppers lightly."

World.title: ‘It’s not OK to steal a charity’: Elon Musk takes stand in blockbuster trial
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyCourts ‘It’s not OK to steal a charity’: Elon Musk takes stand in blockbuster trial Barbara Ortutay April 29, 2026 — 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

California: Elon Musk, the Tesla CEO, world’s richest man and OpenAI cofounder, took the stand on Tuesday (US time) in a high-stakes trial revolving around a bitter feud between himself and former friends Sam Altman and Greg Brockman that could reshape the future development of artificial intelligence. The bickering billionaires’ appearances at the Oakland federal courthouse foreshadow the start of a legal drama that is expected to brim with intrigue and potentially embarrassing details about the two tech moguls. Musk filed the lawsuit against Altman and Brockman along with Microsoft over its investments in OpenAI, in 2024. Elon Musk arrives at the federal courthouse in Oakland, California. AP “Fundamentally, I think they’re going to try to make this lawsuit...very complicated, but it’s actually very simple,” Musk said. “Which is that it’s not OK to steal a charity.” The jury was elected Monday and the trial is scheduled to take three weeks.



Opening arguments began with Musk’s attorney, Steven Molo, who quoted OpenAI’s mission statement when it was created as a nonprofit for the benefit of humanity as a whole and not constrained by the need to generate financial enrichment for anyone. Altman and his top lieutenant Brockman, aided by Microsoft, “stole a charity,” Molo said, “a charity whose mission was the safe, open development of artificial intelligence.” Related Article Opinion

AI AI heavyweights’ court battle could unravel the entire sector Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In the civil lawsuit, Musk, the world’s richest person with an estimated fortune of $US778 billion ($1.08 trillion), accuses Altman and Brockman of double-crossing him by straying from the San Francisco company’s founding mission to be a steward of a revolutionary technology. He is seeking damages and to fund the altruistic efforts of OpenAI’s charitable arm and Altman’s ouster from OpenAI’s board. OpenAI has brushed off Musk’s allegations as an unfounded case of sour grapes that’s aimed at undercutting its rapid growth and bolstering Musk’s own xAI, which he launched in 2023 as a competitor.



In his opening statement, OpenAI lawyer William Savitt told jurors “we are here because Mr. Musk didn’t get his way with OpenAI.” Savitt said Musk used his promises to provide funding to bully OpenAI founding members and tried to take control of OpenAI and merge it with Tesla. In fact, he said Musk wanted to form a for-profit company and own more than 50 per cent of it. In the middle of discussions about OpenAI’s future, he added, Musk pulled the plug on $US5 million quarterly donations he was making. Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, is also expected to testify, along with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, one of the technology leaders who helped fund the late 2022 release of ChatGPT, the chatbot that unleashed the current AI boom. AP There is no record, Savitt said, of promises made to Musk that OpenAI was going to remain a nonprofit forever, or open-source everything. What Musk ultimately cared about, he said, was not OpenAI’s nonprofit status but winning the AI race with Google. Molo said the case is not about Musk, but rather Altman, Brockman and Microsoft.



By 2017, about two years after OpenAI’s founding, it became clear that OpenAI would need more money, and Molo said the founders eventually settled on the idea of creating a for-profit arm of OpenAI that would support the nonprofit. Terms were capped for investors so they “couldn’t make infinite profit.” “There is nothing wrong with a nonprofit having a for-profit subsidiary, but (it) has to advance the mission,” Molo said. “Fundamentally, I think they’re going to try to make this lawsuit...very complicated, but it’s actually very simple. Which is that it’s not OK to steal a charity.” Elon Musk Microsoft initially invested $US2 billion in OpenAI. Then, in 2022, news spread that OpenAI had done a deal with Microsoft and “this was a horse of a completely different colour,” he said. It was a “gamechanger,” Molo said, that violated “every commitment” OpenAI made not just to Musk but to the world. It was no longer open source, it became a for-profit company for the benefit of the defendants and Microsoft was going to have control, through licensing, of much of its intellectual property, Molo said. Musk’s side is expected to present a tale chock-full of alleged betrayal, deceit and ambition that caused OpenAI to pivot from its founding mission as an altruistic startup to a capitalistic venture now valued at $US852 billion.



Related Article Billionaires ‘Crazy and nasty’: Secrets revealed as the world’s richest man and his rival go to war Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, is also expected to testify, along with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, one of the technology leaders who helped fund the late 2022 release of ChatGPT, the chatbot that unleashed the current AI boom that has propelled the stock market to record heights. Altman’s court appearance likely made him unavailable to attend an Amazon event across San Francisco Bay on Tuesday at which both companies announced an expanded partnership. “I wish I could be there with you in person today,” Altman told attendees of Amazon’s event in San Francisco via a prerecorded video message. “My schedule got taken away from me today.” More to come

World.title: Ex-FBI boss Comey indicted again, this time over seashell ‘threat’ to Trump
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaJames Comey Ex-FBI boss Comey indicted again, this time over seashell ‘threat’ to Trump Alanna Durkin Richer and Eric Tucker April 29, 2026 — 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Former FBI Director James Comey was indicted again on Tuesday (Washington time), this time in an investigation over a social media photo of seashells arranged on a beach that officials said constituted a threat against President Donald Trump, according to a person familiar with the matter. The criminal case is the second in a matter of months against Comey and is part of the Trump administration Justice Department’s relentless effort to prosecute political opponents of the Republican president. Former FBI director James Comey. AP The seashells photo was posted nearly a year ago, but the indictment was secured as acting Attorney General Todd Blanche – a Trump loyalist who previously served as his personal lawyer – aims to prove to the president that he’s the right person to hold the job permanently. The fact that the Justice Department pursued a new case against the ex-FBI director months after a separate and unrelated indictment was dismissed could open the government to claims of a vindictive prosecution and to arguments that it is going out of its way to target Comey.



Comey had overseen the early months of an investigation into whether the Republican president’s 2016 campaign had coordinated with Russia to sway the outcome of that year’s election. He was fired by Trump months into the president’s first term, and they have openly feuded ever since. The charges in the latest Comey indictment, confirmed to The Associated Press by a person who was not authorised to publicly discuss the matter, were not immediately known. Comey’s lawyer did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment on Tuesday, and a Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately comment. The image from an Instagram post below which Comey wrote “cool shell formation on my beach walk”. nna\mikala.theocharous The prosecution arises from a May post on Instagram in which Comey shared a photo of seashells he saw on a walk in the arrangement of “86 47”. He has said he assumed that the numbers reflected a political message, not a call to violence. Comey deleted the post shortly after it was made, writing: “I didn’t realize some folks associate those numbers with violence” and “I oppose violence of any kind so I took the post down.”



Nonetheless, Comey was swiftly interviewed by the Secret Service after Trump administration officials asserted that he was advocating the assassination of Trump, the 47th president. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America It’s fine to call the US president a fascist or a despot – but this one line really rattled the White House Merriam-Webster, the dictionary used by the AP, says 86 is slang meaning “to throw out”, “to get rid of” or “to refuse service to”. It notes: “Among the most recent senses adopted is a logical extension of the previous ones, with the meaning of ‘to kill.’ We do not enter this sense, due to its relative recency and sparseness of use.” Trump, in a Fox News Channel interview in May, accused Comey of knowing “exactly what that meant”. “A child knows what that meant,” Trump said. “If you’re the FBI director and you don’t know what that meant, that meant assassination. And it says it loud and clear.”



The former FBI director was indicted in September on charges that he lied to and obstructed Congress related to testimony he gave in 2020 about whether he had authorised inside information about an investigation to be provided to a journalist. He denied any wrongdoing, and the case was subsequently dismissed after a judge concluded that the prosecutor who brought the indictment was illegally appointed. Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush’s Republican administration. Acting Attorney-General Todd Blanche. AP But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum. Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump’s presidential campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, would ultimately find that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.



Blanche was elevated earlier this month from deputy attorney general to acting attorney general, replacing Pam Bondi, who had frustrated Trump with the department’s struggles to build successful criminal cases against his adversaries. Related Article Donald Trump Former FBI director Comey questioned over social media ‘threat’ to Trump Blanche since then has moved quickly to announce politically charged prosecutions, including a case last week against the nonprofit Southern Poverty Law Centre, which is accused by the Justice Department of defrauding donors by paying donors to infiltrate hate groups. The group has denied any wrongdoing. Comey is among many Trump foes to face scrutiny over the last year. The Justice Department, for instance, is also pursuing a criminal investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan, another key figure in the Russia investigation – one of Trump’s chief grievances and a saga that he and his supporters have long sought retaliation for. Brennan has denied doing anything wrong.

With an estimated $5 trillion dollars set to be passed onto the next generation in coming decades, Australians are being urged to think seriously about estate planning. “We’re on the cusp of one of the largest wealth transfers we’ve ever seen,” explains Peter Hogg, general manager guidance and advice at Aware Super. “That’s driven by an ageing population, rising asset values, house prices and superannuation.” Keeping your will up-to-date is of crucial importance. iStock When to make a will It’s common to think you need a certain level of wealth before bothering to make a will, but that’s not the case, Hogg explains.





How to make a will Aware Super’s Peter Hogg There are several ways to make a legal will, but it’s important to be aware that different states can have slightly different regulations. “One of the biggest myths about estate planning is that it’s really expensive and complex,” says Hogg. “And, sure, there are areas where it can get a bit more complex, but for many Australians having a straightforward will can significantly reduce risk and make sure you’re in control.”



Options range from very basic DIY templates that can be downloaded for free, or kits available to purchase online, or engaging a solicitor, which can be especially important in more complex scenarios. Adam Lubofsky, the founder of online will company Safewill says even if your situation seems straightforward, you’re doing a huge favour for those you leave behind by fulfilling this responsibility. “It is going to be more expensive and more time-consuming if there is no will in place,” he says. If you die without a will, called ‘dying intestate’, the government dictates who receives your assets. And once you start the task, you may find there’s more you want to cover than you first imagine. “At Safewill we’ve seen a lot of personalised instructions,” Lubofsky adds. “Whether that’s funeral wishes, specifying exactly what you want your send-off to look like; or pet-care provision; or specific gifts and assets to your loved ones; or leaving part of your estate to charity.”



Adam Lubofsky. Keep it updated Writing a will is one thing, keeping it current across life events and stages is another. “A will is not a ‘set and forget’, ” Lubofsky cautions. In fact, several life circumstances impact the validity of a will, like marriage or divorce … so making sure that you keep it up-to-date is of utmost importance.” “Because if you write a will that isn’t valid at the time it’s surfaced, there isn’t that much point to it.”



Hogg agrees, saying ease of amending documents is crucial: “We would expect that over the course of someone’s life, they might update their estate planning a number of times.” Related Article Sponsored

Superannuation How to calculate your ‘magic retirement number’ Remember - super is different An often-overlooked aspect of estate planning is how super is treated. “Superannuation doesn’t automatically form part of your estate and that means it doesn’t automatically go to your dependents,” Hogg explains. “Your super is paid to the beneficiary nomination named in your super fund, so that makes that a really critical part of the process.”



There are rules around who you can nominate for this role, so check with your super fund – but the process is generally simple. “For our members, you can do it online,” Hogg explains. “It’s called a ‘binding non-lapsing nomination’ so it doesn’t expire, and it takes just five minutes.” Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions.
